A novelistic portrait of not just the tormented, suicidal man at its center but of an entire nation that feels traumatized and corrupted and futureless. Tracing the events that shaped him into the depressed, screaming mess (standing in front of a train waiting for it to hit him) in a
Memento
-ish reverse-chronological structure that slowly and painfully catalogs a series of bad decisions, material conditions and institutional pressures that transformed him from a bright, curious student with a passion for photography and in love with a girl, to a man capable of deeply upsetting military/police/domestic violence, and unable to make any sort of real emotional or romantic connection despite his efforts. Even before you get to the literal Gwangju Uprising stuff it's quite clear that the political/historical context of living under and collaborating with a right-wing martial law dictatorship was the poison that forever changed this generation of men (and the women that were unfortunate enough to come into their orbit) even before the economic crisis. And Lee Chang-dong's choice to start at the bleak ending and gradually sift backwards through 20-years accumulating details that bring the full picture into focus feels done less out of the sadistic misery some might accuse him of than a heart-wrenching desire to go back and change things. Something the cyclical rhyming ending almost suggests is possible. Now that we see the pattern/path, surely we won't make the same mistakes, right? Yet even in a fleeting moment of bliss in this memory of a specific time and place he declares in the opening scene he's going back to, the sound of that unstoppable train of time/progress rattles on. "Life is beautiful... Do you really think so?" A beautiful bummer.

"When you say you've come to do something of human interest, it makes a person wonder whether you're going to do something of interest to other humans, or whether you consider the person human in whom you're interested."

The wandering ronin as noir/western antihero just a straight up great idea, even before you get into Kurosawa's unbelievable control over the movement and geography of his fluid deep focus telephoto lensing/framing, or Mifune's still unmatched levels of screen swag. The two are in such effortless lockstep with each other that his calm, classical camera maneuvering seems to reflect the cool confidence of how this character moves through this hellish environment; a bridge between the old feudal warrior codes and the burgeoning capitalist criminals. Honestly, the entertaining revenge fantasy surface of watching an awesome samurai do limb-slicing action choreography and cleverly manipulate two rival gangs of utter bozos (and then sit back in his tower and watch the amusing chaos unfold beneath him in a single composition) is done with such unostentatious skill and dry humor I think it's easy to come away thinking the surface is all this is. But underneath there is just as angry and sad a depiction of the corrupt economy we've organized ourselves into and the apocalyptic path of death/destruction it's sending us on that you'd see in things like
Seven Samurai
or
High and Low
. As cool as Sanjuro is, and as cathartic as it is to see him violently dispatch these idiots (shoutout Nakadai who gives an awesome performance as the gun-toting psycho) + subtly protect the innocent townsfolk while performatively playing up how he's a bad man only doing it for personal gain, there's a reason as soon as the town is quieter (and hopefully soon kinder) it has no place for him and he moves on. A skilled dealer of death (like a coffin maker) is only useful during wartime, and ultimately "a long life of eating porridge is best."

This is definitely the most watched DVD of my life right here, which I realized a few minutes in when I still had the timing of lines and shots memorized. ("Whoooaaaaa, he stole that guy's pizzas!") Which probably explains why I've not revisited it all that much—it's like I saw it yesterday! Anyway, alongside
Batman Returns
this is still the high point of the entire genre and trend (imo). On top of being a genius at assembling all the kinetic, acrobatic practical + CG setpieces, and throwing some of his horror chops into the mix (the Doc Ock surgery lab massacre sequence legit scared me as a kid, long before I knew what
Evil Dead
even was; the puppetry work, shadows, shrieking sound design my god), what's always been most special about these is how much of an earnest dork Raimi is.
There's a sheer glee and passion for this character on display, and not just what makes him a fun action hero but the human melodrama and humor of his extreme work-personal life balance dilemma. My ideal Peter Parker is a working-class bozo who gets into slapstick antics trying to evade his rent-demanding landlord and has a genuinely heartbreakingly tortured friend/family/love life. He gets his head slapped around by backpacks while already late for his class, he tries to get into poetry while doing his laundry to impress a girl he's already lost, he tries and fails to help Aunt May apply for a bank loan so she won't lose her home... I can't even imagine one of these movies nowadays slowing down enough to be an old-fashioned class drama or romance like this, to have close-ups of characters feeling complicated things the script is actually naturally and intimately exploring, not just briefly pausing between action scenes so they can do a "story" as a vehicle for fan-service and meme-generation. To include details like Aunt May breaking down mid-sentence telling Peter to take the $20 bill for his birthday, or that brief POV shot of him looking in his dingy apartment closet at his two suits, or the sweet and goofy "Raindrops Keep Falling On My Head" rom-com montage. What's most astonishing to see now is that none of the jokes are meta/sarcastic quips either, here they're often physical gags based in character and if they are verbal they're based in the colorful, memorable personalities of the supporting cast. Even in the roles small enough to warrant one scene/line: Campbell's annoying usher, "any more bright ideas?" train guy. Too many to list out. I'm sure everyone's got their favorite.
Molina is also just inspired casting for the sympathetic mad scientist whose genius and ego lead him down a path of miserable and destructive power-seeking, and serves as a dangerously irresponsible counterpart to Peter's selfish (but completely emotionally understandable) desire to sacrifice his power to live an ordinary college kid life. Tobey's big kitchen confession and his gradual realization after it that he owes it to us to be personally punished for the betterment of society, is arguably the most moving this genre has ever gotten. “Sometimes to do what’s right we have to be steady, and give up the thing we want the most. Even our dreams." [Checks notes] The guy who wrote
Paper Moon
wrote this?! And I mean, c'mon, at the end of the day it's the train setpiece... right? Just the greatest of its kind on-screen. It's an astonishing technical feat, Elfman's rousing score goes crazy, but even moreso it gets me misty-eyed about superheroism (a concept this reckons with seriously, sincerely, romantically, philosophically) in the way only this character does for me. "He's... just a... kid." When Dunst literally glows in his apartment doorframe before the "go get 'em, tiger"; a genuinely beautiful image.

For Janus: my notes and interview for THE SAMURAI AND THE PRISONER (黒牢城 / Kokurojo)
“Toss him in the dungeon; do not let anyone see him and do not kill him. Keep him alive until I say otherwise.”
So begins Honobu Yonezawa’s 2021 novel Kokurojo: The Samurai and the Prisoner. The book, which won Japan’s prestigious Naoki Prize, is a work of historical fiction concerned dually with military and psychological warfare; it’s set in Osaka circa 1578 during the Sengoku period, known as the Warring States era.
This backdrop of feudal tensions and fragile factional allegiances contextualizes and heightens a pitched and intimate battle of wills between two men. The Samurai is Lord Akaraki Murashige, a decorated and veteran warrior who presides over the well-fortified walls of the mountain stronghold known as Arioka Castle. His Prisoner is Kodera Kanbei, a cunning emissary of a rival clan. Kanbei has come to Arioka to share his thoughts about the balance of power and how it’s shifting away from Murashige and his supposed allies; his analysis is that the region’s reigning warlord, the ruthless and rapacious Oda, cannot be defeated by any means.
As the bearer of bad news, Kanbei fully expects to be decapitated. His host’s unorthodox decision to take the messenger into custody instead comes not as a relief but an insult—one worthy of some ominous, even cosmic, words of warning:
“If your Lordship commits that which runs counter to the ways of the world…” Kanbei turned a little pale. “Ye shall reap what ye sow”...and thus did the wheel of karma begin to turn.
***
The films of Kiyoshi Kurosawa are about the ways of the world, and how they can turn violently and in unexpected directions. The 70-year old Japanese master has a grip on what it feels like to lose your way, your faith, or your mind; few contemporary filmmakers are more dexterous when it comes to grasping reality and then spinning it wildly off of its axis. His prevailing reputation is as a conjurer of bad karma, from hypnotic serial killers to evil trees to ghosts in the machine; the remarkable 2024 troika of Cloud, Chime, and The Serpent’s Path hinted that, to paraphrase Kurosawa’s student and collaborator Ruyusuke Hamagichi, evil did exist; together they comprised an extraordinary trilogy of terror.
The master of horror label fits Kurosawa even as it belies the true range of his output, and the deceptive elasticity of his style as well. The movie version of The Samurai and the Prisoner—faithfully adapted by the director from Yonezawa’s best-seller—is an outlier in his filmography; it’s also, paradoxically, a culmination, a stately and scenic detour through historical and metaphysical territory that intersects with Japan’s literary and cinematic legacies while plumbing its own subterranean (and contemporary) depths of suggestion. For Kurosawa, form follows function, and Kokurojo is meticulously designed on every level; its spartan interior spaces and treacherously twisty plot lines are labyrinths leading back to a great artist’s singular concerns.
Or, maybe, leading straight to Hell; the inferno serves as a powerful undertow for a story steeped in spiritual and ideological anxiety about the paths of glory and where they might lead. Despite being a period piece—Kurosawa’s first feature set before the 20th Century, against a backdrop familiar classics like Ugetsu and The Seven Samurai — The Samurai and the Prisoner accesses the same grave, apocalypse-now atmosphere as his earlier, turn-of-the-millenium Charisma or Bright Future. For Lord Murashige, perched on a throne of blood and surrounded on all sides by enemies, it is surely easier to imagine the end of the world than the end of the war.
The sense of impending doom is exacerbated by a series of violent deaths in and around Arioka Castle whose strange circumstances hint at demonic forces, or maybe divine intervention. In the absence of reasonable explanations, or anything like a list of suspects, Lord Murashige turns to Kanbei, who’s got a mind for riddles and nothing else to do with his time than play house detective. What’s increasingly uncertain, as the bodies begin to pile up behind the castle walls and enemies begin breaching them, is who’s truly in charge in the dungeon: whether the Samurai is the Prisoner, or vice versa; whether the man in shackles is the one with the upper hand.
Freedom and submission are warring states of mind; so are reason and superstition. “What is this world coming to?” asks one character late in the film. “Nothing makes sense any more.” Like all of the greatest filmmakers, Kurosawa offers up potential explanations only to evade them; the latent, existential confusion on display doubles as proof of lucidity. No less than Cure or Cloud, Kokurojo is a scary movie; it’s also a thought experiment punctuated with a question mark, a parable about the traps we’ve laid for ourselves, and the possibility of escape, while we’re alive, or until somebody says otherwise.
Interview: Director Kiyoshi Kurosawa
Q: How did you come to read Honobu Yonezawa's novel?
A: The novel had won a string of literary prizes in Japan and was very well known. I don't read much fiction myself, so I had no idea about it at all until my producer recommended it to me. That said, I'd been interested in the Sengoku-era warlord Araki Murashige for some time. On my first reading, I realized that this was an unusual kind of book for Japan: a strikingly logical, meticulously constructed mystery novel. It was, of course, tremendously entertaining, and I felt that getting to adapt it into a film myself would be a really meaningful challenge.
Q: The novel combines elements of historical drama and mystery fiction. How do you think these genres come together in Honobu’s writing? And how did you approach the process of adaptation?
A: Because this is a mystery, the story naturally hinges on a crime, a motive, and a method, and those elements are interlocked in such an intricate and precise way that if even one piece were missing, the whole story could collapse. We had to be extraordinarily careful when writing the screenplay. But more than any of the individual criminal puzzles, the greatest fascination of the story lies in the mystery surrounding the protagonist Araki Murashige's own words and actions. The novel's portrayal of him as a character so unlike any conventional Sengoku warlord set my imagination racing.
Q: This is not your first period piece but it is your first film that exists outside of anything like a modern frame. How did you approach this era of history? Were you interested in realism or stylization? Were there films or filmmakers that influenced your depiction of the Sengoku era? Did you try to avoid obvious reference points?
A: I had no intention of inventing a wholly new style of period drama. If anything, I set out to make an extremely orthodox jidaigeki: the kind that's actually quite rare these days. The reason is that I felt a sense of crisis: contemporary Japanese audiences have largely forgotten the great Japanese period dramas of the 1940s and 50s, which I consider the genre's richest era, and what circulates today is mostly period work that's been loosely modernized (which can be perfectly enjoyable on its own terms, as a kind of fantasy). I worry the genre itself may be falling apart. At the same time, I had a contradictory desire: to aim for classical form while telling a contemporary story. In that respect, the real Araki Murashige, who lived in 16th-century Japan, was a man with strikingly modern thinking for his time, which made him an ideal protagonist through whom this film could speak both to the history of cinema and to our present moment.
Q: The structure of the novel and the film are similar in that they move through different seasons; can you talk about the landscape and setting as a character within the novel and the film? And also about the locations: the dungeon is a very abstract space. You’re often associated with modern, urban interiors; how did you approach the architecture, aesthetics and decor of the 16th Century?
A: It's a very interesting question, but a hard one to answer. In all the films I've made until now, I've always wanted the locations to be places that imply a world existing beyond their edges — but this time, that wasn't the case. In a contemporary drama, you can be sure that the real world extends beyond the frame, beyond the windows, beyond the doors. But what is the reality of 16th-century Japan? How are you supposed to make the audience feel that "outside"? In the end, I never figured out what kind of world actually lay beyond the windows of an old Japanese house. Maybe making a period film is, fundamentally, almost the same as making a fantasy. So perhaps the dungeon scene wasn't the only one — every location in this film may in some sense have been an abstract space. But by treating each location as a kind of theatrical stage, I think the crew, the actors, and I were able to find our way to the reality of each scene.
Q: The phrase “advance to paradise, retreat into hell” is very important in the novel; the story begins with it. Do you think that The Samurai and the Prisoner is a story about philosophy? Does the phrase have a political dimension to you?
A: "Advance to paradise, retreat into hell " is a phrase that originates in old Japanese Buddhism, but I think it still applies very much to the present day. Everyone knows how much misery is being scattered around the world by the foolish posturing of those in power who are bound by these very words. And the many people in the grip of the illusion of economic prosperity are bound by them just the same. In that sense, the line that the heroine Chiyoho speaks near the end of the film — "There is paradise even for those who retreat" — has a major influence on Araki Murashige's subsequent actions, and it carries tremendous weight for me as well.
Q: Can you talk about the approach in this film to violence? How do you deal with violence in your staging while still leaving things to the imagination?
A: I've made many violent films over the years, but the truth is that I'm not particularly fond of overt depictions of violence. If you want to see real violence, you can find as much of it as you'd like on YouTube these days — but that isn't cinema. Violence on film, I believe, has to be real and restrained at the same time. You obviously can't unleash actual violence on a set, so any expression of violence has to come into being purely as fiction, as direction, as performance. It's a critical moment that tests the abilities of both the director and the actors. And precisely because it does, the instant you start showing off that craft, a blatant artificiality fills the screen and the viewer is pulled right out of the film. The line between cinematic reality and fiction is paper-thin, and it's the depiction of violence, more than anything, that exposes that line.
Q: Speaking of performance, how did you cast your lead actors? I’m especially interested in Masaski Suda, whose presence is very different here from Cloud even though there’s a certain ambiguity – and maybe menace – that exists between the two roles…
A: Among Japanese actors in their early thirties, there is simply no one besides Masaki Suda who can play a character this ambiguous and complex — someone whose true intentions are impossible to read, who can shift from saint to villain in a single instant. For Araki Murashige, Kuroda Kanbei is at times a partner, at times a servant, and at times something almost demonic. This difficult portrait of Kanbei would have been impossible without Masaki Suda. That said, the real axis of this film is the character of Murashige himself, who is tossed about by Kanbei and yet gradually finds his own path forward — how a man of immense power lets that power go, breaks free of it, and finally attains his freedom. That, I'd say, is the central theme of the film. And Masahiro Motoki played this protagonist, who undergoes a complete 180-degree transformation, to absolute perfection.
Q: Can you talk about the idea of mystery in your work? As an artist, do you identify more with the character of the samurai ( the one who wants to know) or the prisoner, the one who seeks to explain? Or do you see yourself in both?
A: My view is that, in a film, the author has an obligation to provide an answer to every mystery he poses. At the same time, I don't think it's necessary to explain the reasons behind the protagonist's actions. So Murashige goes about solving the various mysteries with great precision, but the reason he eventually walks out of the castle at the end is never explained. Historically, it's a fact that Araki Murashige suddenly left the castle, and I simply depicted that as it happened — but the real reason he did so is something nobody knows. I don't know either, of course.
Q: For audiences who are more familiar with your other, more obviously horror-oriented work, in what ways would you say The Samurai and the Prisoner connects with your earlier films?
A: I'm not a horror specialist; I've always aspired to be a craftsman who can take on any genre. So when an offer came in to make a period drama based on a great novel, there was simply no question of turning it down. I have no interest at all in leaving my own fingerprints on a film. And yet, there may well be some hard-to-hide common thread between the assortment of films I've made over the years and The Samurai and the Prisoner. Finding that thread is always the work of critics and viewers. Time and again, some aspect of my authorial sensibility that I had never given any thought to get suddenly identified — and each time, along with my surprise, I feel a deep sense of satisfaction: I'm so glad I made this film. With this new picture, I'm quietly hoping for the same thing to happen again.

Full-frontal close-ups of babies crowning their way out of the womb have become unexpectedly commonplace since “Knocked Up” popularized the trend some 20 years ago. While these images evoke a measure of body horror, none of them could hope to compete with the gore-mad giddiness of the money shot from the first act of Hanna Bergholm’s “Nightborn.”
Not only does the infant erupt from between its mother’s legs with the force of a cannonball, but the blood that comes out with it splashes onto the baby daddy’s rictus grin as if his wife had just given birth to a giant squib. That said baby daddy is played by Rupert Grint further enhances the scene’s comic exaggeration; while the actor has become a familiar sight to horror fans since graduating from Hogwarts, the smile he maintains in the face of this nightmare reeks of Ron Weasley in a way that can’t help but heighten the wrongness on display. Having children is not for the faint of heart, “Nightborn” wants you to know, and motherhood can be a Shudder-worthy ordeal even when you don’t give birth to a hairy growling demon spawn who chews through its mama’s nipples so that it can feed on her blood instead. But the experience that Bergholm and Ilja Rautsi have scripted for Jon and Saga (Seidi Haarla) to enjoy is a long, long fucking way from normal.
Just how long? Well, that, at its essence, is what this new genre exercise from the director of “Hatching” is determined to figure out for itself. More primal than scary even before it settles into the sheer tedium of raising a newborn, “Nightborn” is consciously — if not satisfyingly — ambivalent as to what kind of horror movie it might be in the end. Despite a few early moments of CGI-enhanced carnage that seem to anticipate a straightforward thrill-ride (e.g., the baby reaches up and rips its grandmother’s hoop earring right out of her flesh), Bergholm’s focus soon begins to cheat a bit closer to the everyday exasperation of “If I Had Legs I’d Kick You” than the progeny from hell mishegoss of “Rosemary’s Baby.” “Nightborn” is ultimately less interested in framing motherhood as a horror movie than it is in exploring why people refuse to see it that way.

The kind of thing its fake-it-till-you-make-it young hero would overconfidently refer to as a bildungs roman (sic), Matt Johnson’s “Tony” is a briny and bittersweet coming-of-age movie about an obnoxious kid so eager to be someone that he tries to skip over the hard work of becoming. Turns out it doesn’t work like that — or at least it didn’t used to.
That said kid will later grow up to be acclaimed chef, bestselling author, and iconic travel documentarian Anthony Bourdain is almost completely irrelevant to the insouciant fun of watching this leather-jacketed leech bounce around Provincetown in the summer of 1975, where he’s looking for anything but experience. Right now, he’s just a 19-year-old Dominic Sessa with an idea for an idea, some big words he doesn’t fully understand, and a pair of nunchucks tucked away in his bellbottoms. Quoth Bourdain in the film’s opening title card: “I was — to be frank — a spoiled, miserable, narcissistic, self-destructive and thoughtless young lout, and badly in need of a good ass-kicking.” In “Tony,” which retains the sincere flavor of street meat despite being factory-processed within an inch of its life, he gets that ass-kicking hard and fast.
The smartest aspect of the film’s script — credited to Johnson, Todd Bartels, Lou Howe, and Matthew Miller — is how framing its lead as such an inveterate self-mythologizer allows “Tony” to distance its version of Bourdain from the legend that he will ultimately become. “No Reservations” neophytes are invited to take the character at face value, while those of us who’ve spent hundreds of hours watching Bourdain eat his way across the Earth can savor how perfectly Sessa’s embodiment mistakes the ingredients of his eventual success. Bourdain was a relaxed-casual ronin with a wandering spirit and a refined taste for the truth; Tony is an arrogant brat so desperate to be Holden Caulfield that he forgets Holden Caulfield was defined by wanting to be Anthony Bourdain.

Eight years of multiverse shenanigans and momentum-killing Disney Plus shows have reduced the Marvel Cinematic Universe from the most reliable money-printing machine in film history to a sadly confused shadow of its former self. But Destin Daniel Cretton’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” — which accepts as its premise that most people can’t possibly remember or care about whatever nonsense has transpired since this mega-franchise split into several overlapping dimensions — offers such a perfect shot at redemption that it threatens to make all the false starts and fuck-ups post-“Endgame” seem like they were part of the plan from the start.
I mean, the film is practically called “We’re Starting Over,” and its drama’s crux hinges on Peter Parker and his beloved MJ clawing away the cobwebs of mass amnesia in a bid to get back to each other. Back to what matters. Back, perhaps, to the sustainable and dramatically satisfying balance that Sam Raimi once struck between Spider-Man’s power (the enduring hold his boyish reluctance has over the public imagination) and his responsibility (making superhero movies profitable and relevant again).
Alas, we are not so back. In fact, “Brand New Day” is only a few degrees of fraudulent advertising shy of “The NeverEnding Story.” Not only does the MCU’s fourth dedicated Spidey outing fail to undo the damage done to its brand since Thanos died in 2019, this dull and downbeat action sequel goes out of its way to epitomize why the mega-franchise has lost so, so much of its sauce over the last seven years. The film meanwhile clumsily slings between a Peter Parker grief drama (trite), a Frank Castle buddy comedy (forced but funny), and a labored set-up for the next few Phases of Marvel character mix-and-match (a triumphant victory for entertainment lawyers everywhere). But back!?! As the late Maya Angelou famously never said: “When someone tells you that there’s ‘No Way Home,’ believe them.”
On a completely unrelated note, here’s something you’d never have guessed from reading that last paragraph: Sony inexplicably waited to screen this 145-minute movie for critics until 7 p.m. the night before its 9 a.m. review embargo, meaning that some of us — hypothetically — might have been forced to hammer out their copy well after midnight because their three-year-old daughter woke up when they got home, demanded they sit at the foot of her bed, and then started crying whenever they tried to sneak out of the room. Hypothetically. Not that you would ever have been able to tell.
Anyway, “Spiderman: Brand New Day” is, at its most functional, a movie about how much it sucks to make friends after college. There’s a reason why high school besties Ned (a briefly goateed Jacob Batalon) and MJ (Zendaya, sharp and heartrending in the scant few moments that Chris McKenna and Erik Sommers’ garbled script invites her character to recognize some kind of emotional truth) stuck close to each other at MIT before co-leasing an apartment in NYC after they graduated.
No such luck for sad ol’ Peter Parker, who’s been left to yearn for his two closest pals over Instagram since they forgot him at the end of their previous film together. He did it for their own protection, but living with hard sacrifices doesn’t come easy, and our friendly neighborhood Spider-Man has learned to cope with his loneliness by obsessively focusing on his unpaid job as a volunteer crime-fighter. The city loves him so much that you’d think he’d just arrested international war criminal Benjamin Netanyahu, but it’s hard for Peter to take in the public’s affection when the only people who ever really knew who he was under the mask no longer remember that he even exists.

Coming back to this one after familiarizing myself with Larry Cohen's unique brand of absurdist satirical writing and independent guerilla B-moviemaking, I found myself this time around getting more out of it, warts and all. Helps too that I finally got around to the "pre-release" cut that puts 30 minutes of pure Cohen personality and weirdness back in. Gotta say, as messy/shaggy as it is and probably correct as the producers at New World were to make him cut this down to a tight 85-minutes they could sell as trashy 80s body horror/50s science-fiction fun about a killer pint of dairy ("It's like
The Blob
meets
Invasion of the Body Snatchers
!"), I quite liked the relaxed pacing and silly corporate conspiracy mission/adventure movie tone. Giving more time and attention to Michael Moriarty's amusingly eccentric turn as the southern (charm) FBI-man-turned-industrial-saboteur for Big Ice Cream, and the collection of oddball friends he accumulates along the way: an unconventionally sweet romance with Andrea Marcovicci's ad exec, the surrogate kid they kidnap/adopt (and help escape his nightmarish 80s TV advertisement home), even briefly becoming a buddy movie with Garrett Morris' "Chocolate Chip Charlie" and Paul Sorvino's fascist, racist army colonel. I don't know if it actually makes it a "better" movie per se, if anything it might even accentuate some of the issues people already have with it. But my personal feeling was that if it's already uneven and strange in its truncated form that speeds towards all its colorful, campy junk food moments of goopy whipped cream leaking out of grotesque contorted prosthetic husks, and fun old-school miniature/matte/stop-motion monster-disaster movie FX setpieces... might as well slow it down, go all the way, and allow it to be the pure absurdist comedy it was originally intended. In letting the caricatured performances, uncanny 80s commercial jingle brightness and broadness of its consumer culture satire linger, occasionally even distract you from the sudden nasty turns it takes. A much easier movie to root for than it is to enjoy, Potsy Ponciroli’s striking but silly “Motor City” strips grindhouse revenge thrillers down to their studs with a dialogue-free wad of pulp fiction in which big muscles, broad tropes, and a badly implemented soundtrack of overused bangers do all of the talking.
Panciroli is a well-meaning throwback artist whose debut feature — the 2021 Tim Blake Nelson western “Old Henry” — was inexplicably atop the Netflix charts last week. Though he takes obvious pleasure in distilling another genre to its most basic essence, the purity of his intentions is muddled by the unrefined clumsiness of his filmmaking. By a setting so blandly digital that a movie called “Motor City” needs a “1977 Detroit” title card to let us know where it takes place. By “American Hustle”-worthy costumes that make the “1977” part comedically redundant. By a plot so broad it feels like you’re watching a shadow play with the lights on, and setpieces that too often strain to compensate for the movie’s gimmick instead of exploiting it.
The whole non-verbal action thing demands a visual stylist at the height of their powers; to judge by John Woo’s significantly worse “Silent Night,” even a past-their-prime genius might be defeated by the challenge. Potsy Ponciroli is no John Woo. It seems like he’s aspiring to be Robert Rodriguez. I hope to one day see a movie that feels like he was happy to direct it as himself. The good news is that “Reacher” star Alan Ritchson doesn’t need words — or a particularly ingenious auteur — to play a compelling ex-con with a score to settle. He just needs to be enormous (always) and sweaty (sometimes), and he’s excellent at doing both of those things here.

And the "fetishist" now a member of a bizarre underground Mishima cult that believes destruction of the human body using machinery is an act of supersoldier (r)evolution. It feels crazy to say this movie is notably less experimental, more "conventionally" action-y, and makes more narrative sense than its predecessor (not really things I wanted or needed out of it), but it's hard to be bothered by that when the filmmaking itself is just so manically unhinged and imaginatively grotesque at this is. The production design, make-up FX and editing in particular are insane. At one point there's a psychedelic flesh-and-metal stop-motion origins of the universe sequence that turns into a perverse, repressed family melodrama flashback to his father teaching him the way of sweaty BDSM gun-sex and violent patricide. The cut from the screaming molten orange fetus to the steely blue skyscrapers... What a picture.

And also to look at some beautiful faces: Sophie Thatcher, Havana Rose Liu, Charles Melton, Kristine Froseth. How about bisexual lighting, high thread-count linens, or a phalanx of fog machines set to eleven? Or a lyrical musical score that sounds convincingly like it was written by the great Italian composer Pino Donaggio (Don’t Look Now, Carrie, Blow Out) and was actually written by Pino Donaggio? Stroboscopic club scenes and pulled-pork gore? Vaporwave vibes and a mysterious, possibly toxic mist encircling Ridley Scott-style ziggurats? An aesthetic that could be described as “Bladee Runner”?
I could go on. Starlets in spandex wielding laser guns. Whispers of incest. Dougray Scott as a louche movie producer named after the lead singer of the New York Dolls. All of it is, apparently, inspired by its creator’s near-death experience following the serendipitous discovery of a “leaky heart.” [Stefon voice]: If you’re a masochistic auteurist trying to test the tolerance you’ve built up over the years to Pusher-man Nicolas Winding Refn’s strain of druggy self-indulgence—and you don’t mind it when a two-hour matinee feels like pulling an all-nighter—you need to visit Her Private Hell. This film has everything.
Or almost everything. There isn’t really much of a story to be found within the humid camp miasma of Her Private Hell. Contrary to popular opinion—i.e. the overwhelmingly negative critical consensus congealed at Cannes, where it premiered conspicuously out of competition—is not necessarily a bad thing. Narrative coherence is not traditionally Refn’s forte; the Danish director is an unrepentant conceptualist who’s typically at his most compelling when severing cause from effect. It’s when this very status-conscious director tries to court the mainstream, as he did in the overpraised and enervating Cannon Films pastiche Drive, that he ends up in the no man’s land of cynical art-grind-house compromise. Flying the freak flag at half mast does him no favors; he needs to go full NWR or not at all.
If it’s possible for a director’s output to be wildly uneven while feeling entirely of a piece, Refn fits the bill. There are no real outliers in his filmography, at least not since he re-invented himself as a slow-cinema adherent after churning out the adrenalized pulp of the Copenhagen-set Pusher trilogy—the series that served as a joint coming out party for the filmmaker and his star Mads Mikkelsen. Pusher has its champions, but the most interesting thing about Refn’s love-it-or-leave-it-sensibility is that no two viewers—from haters to acolytes to agnostics—will agree on what should be kicked to the curb. I myself would hold tightly to 2008’s Bronson, a brooding bare-knuckle biopic featuring a dead-brilliant Tom Hardy in Pagliacci drag—it’s one of the few contemporary performances that squeezes real juice from A Clockwork Orange. I didn’t think much of 2013’s Only God Forgives when it came out, but the schadenfreude of seeing Ryan Gosling on the other side of Drive being brutalized by his Thai co-star Vithaya Pansringarm has endured nicely all the same: the ugly American (or Canadian) posturing on foreign soil loses his hands for trying to act Bangkok Dangerous.
And then there’s Refn’s polarizing 2019 Amazon Prime miniseries Too Old to Die Young. The series, which was cosigned by crime fiction maestro Ed Brubaker, evokes Raymond Chandler and James Ellroy swapping stories in a K-hole and goes further in terms of violence and vision than anything this side of Twin Peaks: The Return. It’s sprawling enough to find room for dirty cops, sex traffickers, cartel bosses, pagan deities, and Hideo Kojima; by turns boring, absurd, laughable, and extraordinary. (For instance: this bit depicting the LAPD as a fraternity of gleeful, self-identifying fascists.) Too Old to Die Young remains undefeated as a spectacular, instantaneous immolation of big-streamer capital. “They took all my marketing money away because they were afraid that the show would reflect badly on Amazon,” Refn said to the A.V. Club about his 13-hour, 18-million-dollar magnum opus.“The rule of fear is very dangerous,” he added. “Amazon released the show, but they said, ‘We will bury you.’ And so they did. However, you can’t bury a diamond.”
The debate over whether Refn is genuinely fearless or just bereft of common sense—if he’s a savant or just an idiot—matters because he’s a signal 21st century filmmaker. He’s an avatar of style-as-substance whose aesthetics transcend subtitles; one edgelord to potentially rule them all. That poster-boy status may be the reason he’s been so antagonistic to his countryman Lars von Trier, the gold standard for modern provoc-auteurs, over the years. Von Trier is a protean talent who’s forcibly inverted the rule of fear so that his anxieties and phobias become reconfigured as epic confessionals. The main reason he’s stuck around through so many cycles of hype and outrage—like when he compared himself to Hitler at a Cannes press conference in the same year Refn upset him for the festival’s Best Director prize with Drive—is because his black comedies are howlingly funny, on purpose. Refn’s immaculately staged atrocity exhibitions are harder to quantify on those terms, however. They’re atmospheric like a room pumped full of cheap perfume and nitrous oxide; if you’re not giggling madly at the narcotized-artsploitation spectacle, you’re either numb or brain dead.
This is the proper headspace in which to begin appraising Her Private Hell, Refn’s first proper feature since 2016’s The Neon Demon, to which it functions as a kind of spiritual sequel. That film starred Elle Fanning as an upwardly mobile young model and would-be movie star who relocated to L.A. and was corrupted by her own status as a glittering, obscure object of desire. It played like a body-horrific-riff on Showgirls, with detours into cannibalism, necrophilia, and witchcraft. The discordance between the script’s putatively feminist conceptual thrust—a critique of sinister beauty standards and bodily commodification co-written by the director with two women—and the voracious appetite of Refn’s camera for nubile starlets in semi-clothed repose placed the onus of interpretation, as it were, on the audience, but it was at least possible to reconcile its stylized vision of Hollywood as a locus of exploitation.
Ostensibly, Her Private Hell is also set within, or adjacent to, the world of filmmaking. Thatcher’s character, Elle, is an actress preparing to shoot a sci-fi comic-book adaptation called Candy Floss, co-starring her ex-best-friend—and current stepmother—Dominique (Liu). Holed up together in a massive downtown hotel’s five-star suite in between production days, they bristle, separately and together, about living behind frenemy lines at the behest of the man in both of their lives. “This movie is going to be hell,” Elle says, in the low, tranced-out cadence that Refn likes to draw out of his performers; rarely has a self-fulfilling prophetess sounded so bored.
For anyone expecting a truly Stygian descent, be forewarned: Refn’s pacing and dramaturgy are as flatlined as ever. To the extent that multiple plotlines emerge—including a parallel narrative featuring Melton as an American GI named Private K stalking through what seems to be postwar Tokyo in search of his kidnapped daughter—they’re all treated pretty much the same way. That also includes the arrival of the so-called Leather Man, the faceless serial killer who serves as the film’s emblem of lurking, incestuous threat. Suffice it to say that in Refn’s fetishistic-cum-cinephilic universe, there’s always room for G-I-A-L-L-O.
If you try to take these characters and situations literally, Her Private Hell is tough sledding; if you start looking at them as free-floating genre signifiers, the film becomes considerably more absorbing. There’s something genuinely startling in the way Refn juxtaposes his ersatz, CGI establishing shots with palpably tactile interiors; the discontinuity is hypnotic. The preponderance of monograms—including a fateful cigarette lighter—both kids and reinforces the idea of authorship. Meanwhile, the slowly accruing parallels between the film’s various father figures—Scott’s sleazy, showbiz patriarch; Melton’s two-fisted avenging angel; the supernatural Leather Man—suggest a woozy sort of structural intelligence.
The common denominator to the different levels of reality here is a surprising and surpassing tenderness: a tacit acknowledgment of the characters’ bruised feelings even as they’re mobilized as fleshy, anodyne auteur playthings. Throughout Her Private Hell, I kept thinking of Greta Gerwig’s Barbie; with his six pack and firmly set jaw, Melton is like a Ken doll who bleeds. “Everyone was representative of a certain fetish, so they were, in a way, like dolls all around me that I could place in different settings, and mold them and have them move and say things.” Refn told The Film Stage. “And that’s very pleasurable.”
Pleasure, of course, is a subjective metric, and its proximity to pain has been noted by philosophers from the Marquis de Sade to Trent Reznor. (Average those guys out and you basically get Nicolas Winding Refn.) The hurt factor of Her Private Hell is real, and yet it’s not quite right to call it punishing; fragile is more like it. It’s easy to scoff at Refn’s faith-healer rhetoric when he says that this film represented his chance to do something good with his new lease on life; the enduring importance of being earnest is undermined by his own propensity to place everything—people, places, sex, death—in quotes. Still, in a film landscape filled with filmmakers eager to please fans and financiers, Refn’s stalwart and bewildering commitment to his gilded-trashy muse—such as she may be—has an anti-heroic dimension. Nobody asked for this film, and nobody really needs it, either. But that doesn’t make it disposable, per se. To say that Her Private Hell is empty is another way of acknowledging its spaciousness; there are worse ways to spend one’s time than gazing into an abyss.

Everything I already loved about Mark Jenkin’s
Bait
–his social-realist class drama about a rural Cornish fishing village as haunting and beautiful Guy Maddin-esque analog artifact—is thankfully continued here in
Rose of Nevada
. Right down to the old-fashioned coastal ritual ASMR ambience and mesmerizingly dreamy, ghostlike folk horror atmosphere that he generates out of the combination of grainy, richly textured hand-cranked Bolex 16mm photography, elliptical non-linear editing and uncanny post-dubbing/sound design that makes it seem like you’re watching something that’s just been excavated from film cannisters that have been lost (at sea) for decades. All that with the added inclusion of another type of film that I love: the science-fiction time loop. In this case, triggered by two struggling young men (a very good George MacKay and Callum Turner) who need work at the precise exact time on old fishing boat from when their village was thriving (socially, economically, etc.) mysteriously reappears and needs new crewman to do all the netting and gutting. It’s a relationship between flesh-and-blood person and metal vessel that generates a series moody procedural fishing sequences that stylistically play like the more “normal” routine sections of
The Lighthouse
(especially all the stuff with Francis Magee’s bearded skipper!), while also sneakily accumulating this unspoken melancholy sense of history; a lonely, longing nostalgia for a lost time these boys have no memory of but are now experiencing through their repetition of its labor/customs like a form of supernatural incantation. I think how ambiguous and strange this is in terms of tone/pace could end up frustrating some, but by the time I understood what was happening—that these boys are being asked by whatever grander force or design is taking place here to sacrifice their personal lives/identities in order to sustain this depressed, dying town—I found myself quite moved and haunted by it.

film_title: Gail Daughtry and the Celebrity Sex Pass
review_text:
For The New Republic
newrepublic.com/article/213109/gail-daughtry-celebrity-sex-pass-beautifully-implausible
Thirty years ago, on a not very special episode of Friends (“The One With Frank Jr.” for the record) Ross and Rachel swapped “Celebrity Freebie” lists: top fives of famous people with whom they would each choose—and be allowed by their partner—to have consequence-free sex. Ever the culture vulture, Ross opted for Isabella Rossellini, leading to the most incongruous Blue Velvet shout-out in prime-time history. Rachel, meanwhile, chose Chris O’Donnell, John F. Kennedy Jr, Daniel Day-Lewis, Sting, and, in a shocker, ex–Hardy Boy Parker Stevenson. The heart, it has been said, wants what it wants.
David Wain’s new film Gail Daughtry and the Celebrity Sex Pass turns on an egregious no-strings-attached mishap, complete with a cameo from the erstwhile Ms. Green. The setting is Wilbur, Kansas, all picket fences and strip malls, where former high school sweethearts Gail (Zoey Deutsch) and Tom (Michael Cassidy) are set to be wed. She’s bubbly and sweet, beloved by her neighbors and beauty parlor clients; he’s gormless and visibly out of his depth. Both are seemingly happy to go through the motions till death do them part. Pre-gaming an author event at their local bookstore, Gail and Tom start hypothesizing about their celebrity freebies; since the writer in town for the signing is Jennifer Aniston—there to hawk a no-frills cookbook of “Sensible Suppers”—they both agree that she’d be a suitable fantasy fling.
Cut to Tom in flagrante delicto a few hours in the back of the store with America’s Sweetheart. “We talked about this,” he pleads to Gail, who’s mortified, as is Jennifer, which doesn’t stop her from arranging to send Tom some DVDs of Friends (he only knows her from The Morning Show). Heartbroken, but determined to get even on her own set of ethical terms—and egged on by her standard-issue sassy best pal Otto (Miles Guttierez-Riley)—Gail puts her game face on. Otto is off to Los Angeles for a hairdressing convention and suggests she tag along. Their target: Jon Hamm, a handsome prince ensconced at the Chateau Marmont.
No sooner have Gail and Otto landed at LAX than they’ve caught a cab ride with Richard Kind, obtained some star maps and learned about the best spots in town to get a burger (McDonald’s), a coffee (Starbucks) and a blow job (Foot Locker). They also accidentally obtain the briefcase of a reigning Mafia queen bee (Sabrina Impacciatore) who has designs on bringing down the global financial system, and is willing to kill the strangers who’ve made off with her documents. Other impediments to Gail’s righteous carte blanche booty call include misfiring hitmen, unctuous personal assistants, and a machine-gun toting “Weird” Al Yankovic, who helpfully tells her and her friends to “eat it” while chasing them off his property.
Suffice it to say that Wain, who once cast Aniston opposite Paul Rudd in 2012’s Wanderlust, does not make realistic, or even halfway plausible, movies. This laxity is his badge of honor, and he wears it well. Where a status-climber like Judd Apatow cultivates a strenuous, and largely disingenuous, naturalism—John Cassavetes by way of SNL—Wain has no use for respectability. He’s yet to abandon the slovenly, see-what-sticks shtick of Wet Hot American Summer (2001), an epochal work that has informed a swath of post-millennial alt-comedy. By sticking to his guns—and also letting them misfire, or shoot blanks—Wain runs the risk of seeming like an inept veteran when he’s actually an old master of his very particular chosen form.
*
Gail Daughtry and the Celebrity Sex Pass is not a good-looking movie: Kevin Atkinson’s cinematography is so hypnotically bland that Main Street U.S.A. and the Inland Empire become virtually indistinguishable from one another. The performances are broad to the point of active mugging; the storyline doesn’t much strain continuity and credibility as leave them to bleed out in a ditch. This is all to the good. Wain and his co-writer Ken Marino, who appears as a veteran paparazzo helping Gail navigate the city of angels, have each worked on plenty of “normal” television and streaming series since their days on MTV’s The State. They’ve had successful careers meeting the industry halfway—especially Marino, who’s usually the funniest part of whatever he’s in. What they refuse to do is make compromises on their own time. Instead, they play a game of (rubber) chicken with themselves and the audience, torquing artificiality and contrivance into its own screwily lucid sort of worldview: a wryly complacent gaze into the pop-cultural abyss.
Wain is often called a satirist or a parodist, which is true for instance of the winking, ruthless Nora Ephron-esque They Came Together (2014), which leaves vintage rom-com tropes to ripen and rot on the New York City pavement. The label doesn’t always fit, however. “I don’t consider Wet Hot American Summer a spoof at all,” Wain told The Film Stage; “it’s just a movie really sourced in actually going to summer camp, and it’s funny.” The skeleton key to unlocking the director’s sensibility—not that it’s necessarily airtight in the first place—might just be Wet Hot’s gee-whiz, summer-stock metaphysics—the wholesome, theatre-kid excitement of getting your friends together putting on a show. Think of the wonderfully sincere sequence where a group of pre-teens perform “Day by Day” from Godspell, an almost enchanted interlude that feels plucked from memory. And then there’s the final act of Wain’s deceptively conventional and Apatow-adjacent 2008 masterpiece Role Models (co-written with Marino) in which the protagonists are finally reconciled by a rousing game of Medieval cosplay—an immersion in
nerd culture enacted with a welcome lack of condescension towards characters and audience.
It makes sense that such an inveterately playful filmmaker would finally get around to riffing on The Wizard of Oz: Victor Fleming’s 1939 classic is the primal scene of Hollywood escapism after all. The sheer slack-jawed obviousness of the references here is part of the point: “Gail Daughtry” inverts “Dorothy Gale” as surely as “Otto” scrambles Toto, and Hamm eventually refers to himself as a wizardly “man behind the curtain.” Within the film’s Emerald City framework, John Slattery, playing a B-list celebrity, serves as a modern version of the Cowardly Lion (“put em up, put em up” he mumbles, shadowboxing in his garage). Ben Wang, playing a Creative Arts Agency rookie, is a scatter-brained Scarecrow manqué, and Marino as the cynical, heartless photographer, has shades of the Tin Man. Slattery’s performance is wonderfully unhinged; he’s funniest when he’s being used as a punching bag, whether rhetorically—as in an uproarious series of text messages narrating his incremental estrangement from Hamm (who’s left his buddy on read for several years)—or literally, as when he gets a hotel room door slammed on his ankle 34 times, each jolt punctuated by its own piercing yelp of “ow!”
David Lynch used to suggest that most of his movies were spiritual remakes of The Wizard of Oz, and Wain’s embrace of low-rent surrealism can feel Lynchian at times; by following a guileless ingenue through a freaky version of “Hollyweird,” Gail Daughtry becomes the director’s Mulholland Drive, right down to the script’s winking anxiety about the perils of show-business-as-usual. There aren’t a lot of comedy directors who are so willing to deal in outright alienation effects, like the repetition-compulsion of Slattery’s battle with the door, or the gratuitously brutal violence of a late action sequence seemingly staged in one of the same locations as Quentin Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. And then there’s the narrator played by the honey-voiced character actor Fred Melamed, who starts out cheerful and folksy about Gail and her friends but begins wearying of the WTF nature of the material around the same time we do. Melamed’s descent into raging dyspepsia is a signal that Wain knows very well he’s wasting his—and our—time and trusts that we don’t mind. There is a fine line between liberated and lazy, and Gail Daughtry refuses to pick a lane on principle. The swerving is the point; the pleasure resides in the egalitarian notion—rooted in the golden rule of improv—that all jokes, including and especially the bad ones, are created equal.
It’s hard to reconcile deliberately half-hearted humor with real emotion, and Gail Daughtry and the Celebrity Sex Pass is deliberately underwhelming both as a love story and as an attack on the culture industry. Wain loves his offhand anticlimaxes; no surprises for guessing that, choosing between a cheating dork on the one hand and Don Draper on the other, our heroine finally chooses herself. But Gail’s parting words sum up the movie, its makers, and their passions so nicely that they bear repeating. “Let’s keep it loose and freaky,” Deutch tells Hamm before they float off together in a hot air balloon, somewhere over the rainbow.
There’s no way De Niro mugs more as Fearless Leader than he does here.

At the exact minute that baby Nino first came into this world, a rocket erupted through the walls of the Beirut hospital where his mother had just given birth — it was 5:05 p.m. Down the hall, just a few seconds later, a different woman gave birth to a little girl named Yasmina, whose cries could hardly be heard over the sound of the explosions around her. That happened at 5:06 p.m.
“A Sad and Beautiful World” is acutely specific about the time, but withholds any concrete information about the date; amid the half-century of intermittent violence that has plagued Lebanon since the start of its civil war in 1975, such incidents have become as cyclical and unspectacular as the seasons. What year is it when this decades-spanning love story begins? It doesn’t matter, and writer/director Cyril Aris (“Dancing on the Edge of a Volcano”) deliberately confuses the point.
Voiceover narration tells us that a massacre took place that day, and the last stretch of the country’s railroad was destroyed. But it also tells us that “on that day we sent a rocket to space,” a reference accompanied by local news footage of the Lebanese Rocket Society launching its first suborbital test flight in the early 1960s. In a place whose people are forced to endure the same struggles as their parents (to paraphrase one of this film’s most aching laments), time will always be a flat circle. Joy will always be braided together with pain. Fireworks will always be mistaken for bombs. Home will always be a history to escape.
Per the contradiction of its title, “A Sad and Beautiful World” is constantly navigating between a love for Lebanon and the longing to leave it behind, a dialectic that Aris expresses by offsetting the gravity of his film’s setting with the lightness of a pop romance. Imagine if “(500) Days of Summer” was projected onto the pain of life during wartime — or vice versa — and you’ll have a rough idea of how this movie frames the star-crossed relationship between its fated lovers. They remain bound to each other even as their imagined paths to happiness seem to lead in opposite directions.

film_title: A Short Film About the Long Career of Abel Ferrara

review_text:
A solid novelistic British heist film that can’t quite keep up with the Bob Hoskins and Michael Caine crime-thrillers of its era but has some charm and elegance to it. The first half was a bit too dry and sleepy for me personally, a little in part due to its interesting choice to focus on a middle-aged middle-class computer programmer as its protagonist (a neat idea and well-performed by Bernard Hill but after the 7th scene of watching him be drunk and sad and try to connect with his stepson I was zoning out a bit), but more due to what feels like a made-for-TV mini-series leisurely stateliness that sucks some of the air out of the tense situation he finds himself in; namely being kidnapped and made to hack his banks computer system to help out some ruthless criminals. Improves a lot when he cracks the code and is forced to go along for the full
Rififi
mode holiday season bank robbery. All the moderately dull, mannered realism of the style merges with the granular authenticity of how these old sweaty British crooks pull off their stressful job: complete with security system gadgets, gruesome elevator mistakes,
Thief
thermal lances, gasmasks, bizarre getaway driving tactics, etc. It’s a really well put together sequence, and even as its barrel towards how this violent action is going to crossover with the cliché emotional subplot about Found Family or whatever, it’s cool that the hero is a computer nerd who primarily uses planning and engineering to get out of the holes he digs himself into.

Roger Vadim’s strangest American movie is simultaneously a horny dark comedy, a sports movie and a murder mystery — and somehow, successful at being each of them, at least until he is put into the unenviable position of having to deliver a satisfying conclusion (even if its final minutes manage to feature both a football game

Remember when movies used to be comedies, and many of them — borderline most — were about someone trying to save their beloved fraternity house/record store/understaffed gym/Good Burger location from being usurped by corporate scum or other such bullying assholes? “The Dink” sure does, even if it adds a few new wrinkles to that classic formula.
The humbly winsome tale of an arrogant loser who fights to stop his father’s prestigious tennis club from being perverted by the insidious popularity of pickleball (only to realize that he’s playing on the wrong side of the court, so to speak), this fun and breezy lob of a Jake Johnson vehicle pays winking homage to its outmoded tradition with a story that never misses a chance to make fun of its own low stakes. But it would be in bad taste for streaming comedies to piss on the graves of the subgenres they’ve helped to kill, and I’m happy to report that “The Dink” — cleverly scripted by “Hollywood Handbook” co-host Sean Clements, and directed by “Strays” vet Josh Greenbaum — has nobler intentions in mind.
Indeed, the film’s greatest strength lies in how well it leverages such gentle self-parody into the stuff of real sincerity — how well its silly plot reflects and transcends the pettiness of its lead character, and in turn makes a convincing argument for the unembarrassed pleasures of yesteryear, when people were less afraid to look stupid, and maybe didn’t feel like they had to swing so hard in order to score points. Which is to say that “The Dink” isn’t just pro pickleball; it is pickleball. And pickleball seems like a pretty good time.

For Ringer:
www.theringer.com/2026/07/17/movies/the-odyssey-review-christopher-nolan-matt-damon-anne-hathaway
The Odyssey
When Christopher Nolan directed his microbudget debut Following for £10,000 in 1998, he was Nobody, and he knew it. The film was an ingenious, noir-tinged parable about stifled ambitions, with the director splitting himself between a pair of disparate yet strangely sympatico protagonists: a struggling, socially inept cipher living vicariously through the lives of others, and a smooth operator with a gift for the long con.
The archetypes of the manipulator and mark have endured, to varying degrees and in different configurations, in Nolan’s work ever since. To paraphrase a certain Gotham City supervillain, they complete each other. Lately, he’s been fusing them together under the sign of hubris—his great theme, and increasingly resonant in light of his maturation from anonymous craftsman into above-the-title auteur. The potent pulp of Nolan’s salad days has been steadily transubstantiated into prestige; from Batman and 2001: A Space Odyssey to Operation Dynamo and the Manhattan Project, there’s nothing he can’t remake in his own idiosyncratic IMAX-sized image.
The self-reflexive subtext has gotten thicker as the films have gotten bigger. Both Leonardo DiCaprio in Inception and Robert Pattinson in Tenet were legible as floppy-haired stand-ins for their creator, while the read of Oppenheimer as a parable about the collaborative nature of filmmaking—including the devil’s bargains of financing and owning intellectual property—was very much there for the taking. The stakes felt higher than portrait-of-the-artist vamping, however. The sobering power of Oppenheimer lay in its shift away from the James Bond-style intrigue of Tenet, in which the fate of the planet hung outlandishly in the balance, and towards a very real world in the process of watching itself burn. Not that Nolan’s adaptation of American Prometheus left myth behind, exactly. The film’s processional-procedural structure barely belies a tragic, allegorical design; Cillian Murphy’s expression in the coda suggests a genius reckoning with the carelessness of leaving Pandora’s Box ajar.
Whatever its flaws, Oppenheimer met and exceeded its paradoxical mandate as an apocalyptic period piece: a flashback to the beginning of the end. With The Odyssey, Nolan’s reach is even broader, extending for the first time beyond a modern frame. The opening title card places us in the Bronze Age, described a “time of apparent magic”—a designation recalling the agnostic backdrop of The Prestige, whose duelling illusionists were caught, along with their audience, in a double bind between science and superstition.
Nolan hasn’t secularized The Odyssey, exactly: There are malign sorcerers and slimy sea creatures and a voracious, dinosaur-sized Cyclops who gnaws the heads of Ithacan infantrymen like pitted green olives. Like any good theme park mogul, Nolan has spared no expense. But even as the filmmaker makes his first plunge into all-out fantasy—including an extended and stomach-churning foray into body horror on the isle of Aeaea, whose witchy proprietress (a stellar Samantha Morton as Circe) has a you-are-what-you-eat policy—there’s a sense of judiciousness, or even austerity. There’s a wariness of spectacle for its own sake.
Is this a nice way of saying that The Odyssey, which arrives as this summer’s designated big-budget auteur-de-force, isn’t that much fun? Maybe. Nolan isn’t the guy we go to for weightless excitement, anyway, the time-travel hijinks of Tenet notwithstanding. There’s always a lecture on the docket, delivered with a deep voice and a furrowed brow by some British thespian or other. “Theatricality and deception are powerful agents to the uninitiated,” caterwauled Bane through his BiPAP in The Dark Knight Rises. Nolan, who’s obsessed with sleight-of-hand—and good at it in his nimblest pictures—sees that rhetoric and raises it interestingly in The Odyssey. He’s fascinated and mortified by the power of self-deception, and the massive collateral damage that comes from playing with fire.
Exhibit A: the promise made by Matt Damon’s genius military strategist-slash-homecoming-king Odysseus to return to his family no matter the cost. And why wouldn’t he want to? His wife, Penelope (Anne Hathaway) is a model of competency and constancy who has sworn to reject the advances of any and all suitors in her husband’s absence. That includes denying the sexily leering Antinous (Robert Pattinson), who’s not above strutting around the castle like he owns the place. And then there’s Odysseus’s staunch and solid son Telemachus (Tom Holland),—a chip off the old marble block, if not exactly a commanding personality. The latter’s desire to find out whether his wayward dad is still alive after a decade at sea, which involves confabbing with the brutish king Menelaus (Jon Bernthal) in Sparta drives one side of the narrative. Odysseus’s harrowing journey in the company of his stalwart—though steadily dwindling—crew after their successful siege of Troy drives the other. When our man isn’t battling monsters or staving off mutiny, he’s visited by visions of goddess-of-wisdom Athena (Zendaya), a morosely beautiful avatar of female judgment in the best Nolan tradition (and another link to Oppenheimer, although it’s not worth spoiling the conceptual twist behind her role).
“I will defy the Gods,” mutters Odysseus when he’s informed by his spirit guide that Zeus and co. aren’t likely to grant him and his men safe passage. His obstinacy towards the powers-that-be is pure arrogance; it also belies the fact that he’s already done their dirty work as a destroyer of worlds. Suffice it to say that this version of The Odyssey is only interested in heroism so far as it can deconstruct it; its namesake’s sense of barely sublimated guilt—the moral stain that means no amount of ocean spray will wash the blood off his hands—provides a baseline for Damon’s commanding lead performance. There have been some famous screen Odysseuses, including Frederic March and Kirk Douglas, both of whom led with their broad, bare chests; there’s a tendency for alpha-male-movie stars to cultivate vanity when in sword-and-sandal mode. Damon’s wilier than that, though, and despite looking rather ripped, he never seems to be posing for his own bronze bust (or lobbying for an Oscar). Having long since ceded the action-hero territory he briefly cornered as Jason Bourne, he opts instead for a brawny melancholy, which serves to well anchor a movie leveraging escapist thrills against the rough-hewn realism of a physically demanding location shoot.
“It was by far the hardest movie I’ve ever made,” Damon told GQ, which is standard-issue stuff for the PR circuit. Stories about battling the elements and pushing bodies to the limit helped Leo score his Oscar for The Revenant. Nevertheless, the bruised-and-battered anecdotes line up with the tactile physicality of the onscreen product, which mostly achieves the desired grandeur. The Mediterranean skies and seas in The Odyssey serve as naturally occurring special effects, with hills and valleys that feel uncanny by their own account. Pictorially speaking, this is probably Nolan’s most purely beautiful movie, shot by Hoyte van Hoytema as a series of vast yet startlingly granular panoramas; for every composition that recalls one of the director’s earlier films—beachfront military formations straight out of Dunkirk; a decapitated marble head rolling to rest like one of the top hats from The Prestige—there are images and sequences that feel conjured out of thin air.
Of course, for $250 million dollars, you’d expect The Odyssey to look good. Operating with the Olympian resources to ship a boatload of A-listers to Peloponnese for thunderbolt practice, Nolan indulges his usual showmanship while also weaponizing it, the same way he did in Oppenheimer. There’s a difference between the gruelling, wholly unintentional sloggery of Nolan’s Batman movies and the calculated alienation effects of Oppenheimer and The Odyssey, which are grim in ways that imperil their respective price tags—the trade-off, perhaps, being the same inflated critical currency that Steven Spielberg or Quentin Tarantino started accruing when they decided to grow up and get serious.
Nolan has always been pretentious, and he hasn’t always made this quality sing for him. The Odyssey, though, answers the rhetorical question of “why so serious?” with a straight face and a bleeding heart on the sleeve of its carefully embroidered tunic. It’s about as angsty and anxious as a movie made at its industrial level can be, and its concerns, however obliquely expressed, lie in the present tense. Nolan has taken his studio’s money and put it where his mind is at: a good strategy for being taken seriously. Like Steven Spielberg in Disclosure Day, he’s gesturing towards certain geopolitical realities without directly naming them. Take your pick whether that's subtlety or reticence. The Odyssey isn’t moving, exactly, but it is powerful as a byproduct of a filmmaker choosing to stick to his guns (or his crossbow). It gives us one of the greatest stories ever told reimagined as a cautionary tale; the blockbuster as a dark-hued Trojan Horse.
Speaking of which: That equine vessel works wonderfully as an iconographic set piece, introduced half-buried in the surf like the Statue of Liberty in Planet of the Apes. (When we get a look inside, it’s basically a chamber of horrors—an iron maiden flooding from the sand up). The casting of Elliot Page as Sinon—Odysseus’s most loyal soldier, famous for adopting the guise of a deserter in order to convince the Trojans to accept his boss’s booby-trapped offering—is smartly pressurized by the actor’s earlier appearance in Inception. Here, Page becomes an anguished emblem of sacrifice instead of a dreamweaver. The word is that Nolan used Oxford scholar Emily Wilson’s controversial 2017 translation of The Odyssey—the first ever authored by a woman in English verse—as a scaffolding for his screenplay, but he’s no more reverential to Wilson (or Homer) than he was to Bob Kane. “Feel free to add things,” says Sinon to Odysseus by way of granting him posthumous poetic license over their life and deeds; between the colloquialness of the language and the permissiveness of the sentiment, this throwaway line could well be Nolan’s skeleton key.
“No one in history has ever done anything this clever,” said another Homer once while proffering a suspicious peace offering of his own to his enemies. Suffice it to say that at 172 minutes, The Odyssey lacks the satirical compression of “Lemon of Troy,” and similarly isn’t trying for the wiseacre pastiche of O Brother, Where Art Thou?, still the gold standard, along with its spiritual sequel Inside Llewyn Davis, of imaginative Odyssey iterations. Nolan is not exactly a cut-up even when his movies are funny (i.e., Guy Pearce forgetting who’s chasing who in Memento or John David Washington getting impatient over hot sauce in Tenet) and he’s tamped down on the bawdy, proto-picaresque tone of the source material. The film is mostly sexless and bereft of jokes, even as Pattinson’s mealy-mouthed cowardice grows pretty amusing by the end. Talking with Jon Stewart the other night, Nolan balefully explained that he excised a crucial exchange between Odysseus and the Cyclops in which the latter is informed that his captive’s name is “Nobody” and ends up making a fool of himself when trying to identify the guy who’s blinded him with a stick—a bit of shtick that might have made for a hilarious set piece. Stewart relayed the frustrations of his viewing companion, whom he described as a stickler for details. “He was very upset that [the joke] was not in the movie.” “Puns in translation are tough,” Nolan replied. “I tried.”
He did. It’s probably somewhere between a compliment and a critique to say that The Odyssey reeks of effort—honest exertion rather than flop sweat, but redolent all the same. When Nolan is at his very best—like in Memento and The Prestige, or the most pressurized passages of Dunkirk or Tenet—he works up an intense but ineffable sense of convergence; Inception’s indelible image of a metropolis implacably folding in on itself summarizes his gift for stratifying narrative across multiple planes of time and space. The Odyssey is edited by Oscar-winner Jennifer Lame, who sutured together Oppenheimer’s color-coded plotlines, and yet it moves only in fits and starts, slacking noticeably when it’s focused on Tom Holland’s sullen teen who would be king act or Charlize Theron’s soporific Calypso. (The passages of Odysseus’s lotus-eating are so close tonally to the amnesiac metaphysics of Memento that you can feel Nolan’s delight in using Homer as an excuse to take a victory lap). For all the (idiotic) online furor over Lupita Nyong’o’s Helen of Troy, she’s a marginal presence, introduced with her ship-launching-features already disfigured by her jealous husband; as for Benny Safdie’s Agammemnon, he’s barely visible behind his iron mask.
There’s a brief moment at the outset of The Odyssey, set during a kind of Grecian slam poetry reading, where it appears we might get a truly digressive, multifaceted retelling of Homer’s story: an impressionistic amalgam of perspectives creating Odysseus in unreliable aggregate as per the oral tradition. Nolan feints in that direction—he does love his elliptical insert shots—but mostly keeps his point of view reliable and the pacing conventional; functional choices that become ironic insofar as he finally styles the whole enterprise as a meditation on storytelling. The last sequence finds Odysseus reflecting on his legacy and how he’ll be remembered by later generations; he tells Penelope that one day, people will be listening to songs about them. Cue “When I’m Home,” by Travis Scott and James Blake. Sing, O Muse!
This was The Odyssey in the Duffield household this weekend.
